PHSCS 587

Poisson equations and scale length

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how a dominant electrostatic eigenmode attenuates with channel length

In a depleted region with prescribed fixed charge, Poisson’s equation is linear. One can split the potential into a particular solution for that charge and homogeneous solutions that enforce source, drain and gate boundary conditions. This superposition does not apply unchanged to arbitrary nonlinear carrier populations.

Separation of variables gives electrostatic eigenmodes. In the reading’s convention, the leading contribution to the minimum channel potential contains exp[−πL/(2λ₁)]. Larger L/λ₁ suppresses contact influence. Both the exponent convention and the omitted voltage-dependent prefactor matter.

If a decay length ℓ is defined by a spatial factor exp(−y/ℓ), it corresponds to λ₁/π for the stated mode, not λ₁ itself. A symmetric double-gate approximation ℓ ≈ √[εsi tsi tox/(2εox)] is a limited thin-angle model; exact dielectric boundary matching retains geometric floors and must be used before extrapolating to extreme high-κ oxides.

Example

Increasing L/λ₁ from 2 to 4 changes the displayed factor by exp(−π) ≈ 0.0432, a reduction of about 23 times. This compares the exponential only, without claiming an extracted threshold shift.

Practice

1. Why can two books quote different scale-length formulas without necessarily disagreeing?

Check the length definition inside the exponential and the assumed boundary geometry.

They may define an eigenlength or a spatial decay length with factors such as π between them. Geometry, dielectric matching and approximation limits may also differ; compare complete exponents and assumptions, not symbols alone.
